whyTheHarvestNotTheInventory: The 150-row inventory is EXHAUSTED for winnable rows. Measured 2026-09-27 against 529 posts on disk and 905 live: only 48 rows remain unwritten and non-gated, of which 9 fail Gate 2 (image gallery / tool page / product landing - a blog cannot rank in those SERPs), 35 are D-listicle (the shape that ABORTED in Brazil at 1-weak-in-8 and measured ten national magazines on de-de, and which was dropped wholesale from wave 1 on that evidence), and only 4 are A/B tier - two of which were already excluded deliberately as redundant with written siblings. laneWideFindings.A-reply-song-contamination: MEASURED TWICE, TREAT AS A LANE-WIDE HAZARD: the bare 'I miss you too' phrase is a SONG TITLE in multiple languages, so the head keyword is often an entertainment SERP and a Gate 2 page-type mismatch. Spanish 'yo tambien te extrano' measured 9 of 10 music (Sebastian Yatra) and recorded Gate 2 as PARTIAL; Russian 'ya tozhe skuchayu po tebe' measured 5 of 8 music (Ramil Mulikov) plus a books.google/litres panel for a novel of the same title, a Spotify entity panel and a YouTube carousel above rank 1. NEITHER aborted, and both were right not to, because the ADJACENT REPLY INTENT is open and weak: Russian measured 'chto otvetit na ya skuchayu po tebe' at 10/10 weak (four domains carrying the SAME syndicated article). WHAT REMAINING REPLY ROWS MUST DO: measure the bare phrase, and if it is music, say so plainly, retarget to the reply/meaning tail, and record Gate 2 as PARTIAL rather than pretending the head term is winnable. Do not abort solely for this - but do not claim the head term either. THIRD CONFIRMATION AND A WORKING FIX: Portuguese measured the unquoted head phrase at 7 of 18 music (Ferrugem, Marilia Mendonca, Amado Batista, Spotify), then RETARGETED to the keyword WITH 'tambem' and music dropped to ZERO, with the quoted SERP 14/14 weak and zero Portuguese editorial. That is the pattern to copy: the particle itself is the disambiguator that clears the music. *** THE PORTUGUESE FIX DOES NOT ALWAYS WORK - GERMAN COUNTEREXAMPLE. *** Adding the particle failed for German because Helene Fischer's 2007 track is literally 'Und ich vermiss dich auch' - the particle is already IN the song title. Its head SERP was 14 results: 5 music, 5 Netflix/TV (Harlan Coben 'Missing You'), an image pack, zero dictionaries. What DID clear it was adding a REPLY-INTENT word ('antwort'): 7 results, 6 weak, ZERO music, Gate 4 PASS. SO THE GENERAL RULE IS: add a word that names the INTENT (antwort / co odpowiedziec / que responder / what to reply), not necessarily the particle. Confirms the aborted German row's finding that de-de is query-SHAPE dependent.
laneWideFindings.A-reply-cross-linguistic-result: The reply question has now fallen FOUR different ways, each proven from that language's own authority, which is a genuinely original cross-linguistic result no single competitor page has: ITALIAN - anche selects what it PRECEDES (Treccani anche 1.a, its own two examples being the minimal pair; De Cesare config. I = NS), so the reply is unambiguous where English is not. FRENCH - the OPPOSITE: aussi takes WIDE scope, the same cell as English also, because both arguments of tu me manques are clitics and a clitic cannot host it (De Cesare fn. 17); French gets precision from subject reduplication instead, used 71% of the time. SPANISH - a CLEAN NEGATIVE: neither RAE work states a positional rule and the DPD's own two citations sit on opposite sides of the target. RUSSIAN - tozhe selects what FOLLOWS it in the sense that it always follows its associate (35/35, 0 preposed), the mirror of Italian, and Russian disambiguates where English cannot. Each row also found a DIFFERENT counter-trap: anche a me manchi means something else; «Tu me manques a toi aussi» literally says you are missed by you too; «a mi tambien» answers me haces falta not te extrano (48 sentences, not one with the speaker as nominative subject). Later reply rows should test their language against this set and cross-link, not restate it. FIFTH ANSWER - PORTUGUESE: position is FREE and ACCENT decides. Alfa: Revista de Linguistica (UNESP) 68, 2024, read in full, presents 'Joao foi na festa tambem' and 'Joao tambem foi na festa' as two POSITIONS of one particle, says the additive tambem 'apresenta maior liberdade sintatica', and following Krifka 1998 gives a pair with IDENTICAL word order, different phrasal accent and a different target. Consequence: in writing, 'sinto sua falta tambem' is as ambiguous as English, and the overt subject pronoun in 'eu tambem' is the ONLY written disambiguator. Portuguese also does NOT have the Spanish dative counter-trap - four checks: 'a mim tambem' 0 vs 141 for bare 'a mim'; Priberam's /pt-br/falta has no 'fazer falta' locution at all; Michaelis defines it around 'a PESSOA MORTA' (bereavement); and Michaelis PT-EN glosses 'eu tambem' as 'So am I', i.e. NOMINATIVE, the opposite of Spanish. And the French reduplication trick FAILS twice over in Portuguese: there is no subject to duplicate, and 'Voce tambem' collides with a documented expressive 'tambem' carrying 'um conteudo de desaprovacao' - the trick lands on a reproach. SO THE TALLY IS: Italian position-selects, French wide-scope-clitic-blocked, Spanish no-rule, Russian always-follows, Portuguese free-position-accent-decides. FIVE languages, FIVE mechanisms, each from that language's own authority. SIXTH ANSWER - DUTCH: scope is carried by the PRONOUN FORM, not position. ANS 5.2.7 punt 2 names 'ook' inside its own rule - the full form 'jou' is obligatory when the pronoun is accompanied by a particle like ook that has it as its bereik - and prints a minimal pair (haar/'r) distinguished only by form and stress. So a typed Dutch reply disambiguates where a typed Portuguese one cannot, because Portuguese needs accent and Dutch encodes it in the word. Two corrections to my framing, both from ANS: Dutch DOES have the Italian pre-argument slot (21.4.9.4.1 s3, 'voor of na het element'), and the FRENCH REDUPLICATION is the clean negative (21.8 licenses 'alleen dat en die', no repeated personal pronoun) - Dutch does the job in one slot instead: 'Jou mis ik ook'. V2 lever: in a bijzin the first position is gone and the pronoun form is the ONLY disambiguator left. SEVENTH ANSWER - POLISH: ACCENT, not direction. Poradnia PWN nr 12061 (Banko, skladnia, via Wayback) gives a rightward written default - the particle refers to the element 'nastepujacy po niej' - and then states its OWN override in the same answer, when the right neighbour cannot carry the sentence stress, in which case the target PRECEDES. So rightward adjacency is a default that yields to accent. It is the exact COMPLEMENT of French: French aussi has only clitics available to host it, while Polish has a strong form for every clitic, 'za' forces one, and 'ja' has no clitic counterpart at all - Poradnia nr 24530 rules that short pronoun forms cannot open an utterance because that is where the logical accent falls. NKJP confirms: 29 utterance-initial 'Mnie tez', 0 'Tez mnie'. And tez/takze/rowniez is a REGISTER split, not a scope one - NKJP near-parity (330,005/258,151/195,786) against Tatoeba 7.2:1 for tez, same trio, opposite profile - with one hard asymmetry: tez never precedes a nominative pronoun (0 of 352) but takze does. TALLY: Italian position-selects, French wide-scope-clitic-blocked, Spanish no-rule, Russian always-follows, Portuguese accent-decides-position-free, Dutch pronoun-form-encodes, Polish rightward-default-overridden-by-accent. SEVEN languages, SEVEN mechanisms. EIGHTH ANSWER - GERMAN, AND IT CONTAINS THE OTHERS. Berchio, Bonvin & Berthele 2025, JESLA 9(1) 85-102, read in full: German licenses TWO positions of auch, left-of-entity and post-finite. Post-finite is 'non-grammatical in Italian'; 'French shares the post-finite position with German'; left-of-entity 'is not shared with English'. So preposed = Italian, postposed direction = Russian, multiple candidates resolved by accent = Portuguese (same Krifka), postposed preference = French/English, and no rule forcing the reading = Spanish. German has all five sorted by construction and PREFERS the ambiguous one (~30% left-of-entity). Practical payoff unique to German: postposed auch reaches LEFT, so the nearest associate is 'dich' (accusative, the MISSED) in 'Ich vermisse dich auch' but 'mir' (dative, the MISSER) in 'Du fehlst mir auch' - so the second construction puts the particle next to the right person for a reply. Also: 'ich auch vermisse dich' is UNGRAMMATICAL (IDS: focus particles may not stand alone in the Vorfeld). And the commonest German reply is neither - it is the bare ellipsis 'ich dich auch', 457 of 644 inspected hits (71%), about 8x the full form.
